claim_hierarchy.claim: Near-complete Ross aggregate recovery was a loss-weighted average of strongly unequal local restoration and did not restore the pre-disturbance spatial composition.
claim_hierarchy.boundary: All focal path-versus-state and local-restoration decompositions are post-result.

claim_hierarchy.claim: High inverse-path fidelity co-occurred with weak or negative state restoration in all three complete Ross down-up episodes.
claim_hierarchy.boundary: Episodes are descriptive within-series calibration, not independent replicates.

claim_hierarchy.claim: Persistent decline at Palmer and Signy reweighted breeding structure beyond proportional thinning.
claim_hierarchy.boundary: Specific vital-rate mechanisms are not identified.

claim_hierarchy.claim: Beaufort growth after capacity release reweighted breeding structure beyond proportional expansion while independent inter-island export declined.
claim_hierarchy.boundary: Census and movement evidence are independent streams, not mediation.

claim_hierarchy.claim: Unequal local recovery can produce apparently complete aggregate recovery while changing spatial dominance and redundancy.
claim_hierarchy.boundary: The focal field result is post-result and does not establish a universal threshold for local-recovery heterogeneity.

exact_identity.aggregate_restoration: A = sum_i L_i q_i / sum_i L_i
exact_identity.interpretation: Aggregate restoration is the loss-weighted mean local restoration ratio; path mismatch is a loss-weighted measure of local-restoration heterogeneity.

main_sentence: Near-complete aggregate recovery was produced by differential local recovery, so the population recovered where it had declined but not in the same proportions.
withdrawn_claims: Ross restored or re-expressed the pre-shock spatial state
high inverse-path fidelity implies state restoration
near-complete aggregate recovery means most breeding components nearly recovered
the focal result demonstrates latent spatial memory
the 9.41% mismatch is biologically minor because it is numerically small
